passage: I'm Asif, and I live across from Vasudha's family. She's about two. Whenever the pressure cooker whistles, she drops everything and covers her ears, face scrunched. At her cousin's birthday she clung to her mother's leg for a long time before joining the others. Her cousin, the same age, runs straight into any crowd. I don't know what Vasudha feels inside, but loud sounds and new places seem to hit her harder.

qa.q: What does Vasudha do when the pressure cooker whistles?
qa.a: She drops everything and covers her ears, face scrunched.

qa.q: What might Vasudha's clinging at the birthday suggest?
qa.a: It might suggest she needs more time to feel comfortable in new, busy places.

qa.q: How could Vasudha's parents support her?
qa.a: They could give her time to warm up and warn her before loud sounds.

qa.q: How does Asif see the difference between Vasudha and her cousin?
qa.a: Asif notices her cousin runs straight in while loud sounds and new places seem to affect Vasudha more.

grounding: A neighbour observes a toddler's sensory sensitivity and slower adaptability compared with a cousin.

passage:
Monday: Yusuf screamed when Shreya put on his new wool sweater, tugging at the neck.
Thursday: At the mall, he burst into tears at the music. Shreya carried him outside, where he calmed.
Two weeks later: Shreya chose soft cotton shirts and planned a quieter family visit. Yusuf played happily, only covering his ears once when the doorbell rang.

qa.q: What did Yusuf tug at on Monday?
qa.a: He tugged at the neck of his new wool sweater.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf burst into tears at the mall?
qa.a: The loud music seemed too much for his senses and upset him.

qa.q: What changes did Shreya make to help Yusuf?
qa.a: Shreya chose soft cotton shirts and planned quieter visits to suit his sensitivity.

qa.q: How might Shreya's view of Yusuf have changed over these weeks?
qa.a: Shreya may now see his reactions as his sensitive nature rather than naughtiness.

grounding: It shows a toddler's sensory sensitivity and a caregiver adjusting to his temperament over time.

passage: At the colony park in Hyderabad, the new sprinkler burst on. Bhavna, two, shrieked with joy and ran straight in, soaking her frock. Her twin, Alka, stopped at the edge. She held out one finger, touched a drop, then pulled back and watched. Mummy sat beside her. After a long while, Alka stepped in, just one foot.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do when the sprinkler burst on?
qa.a: She shrieked with joy and ran straight in, soaking her frock.

qa.q: What does Alka touching a drop and pulling back suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she is cautious and needs time to test new things before joining in.

qa.q: How did Mummy support Alka?
qa.a: She sat beside her and let her take her time rather than pushing her in.

qa.q: Why might Bhavna and Alka react so differently?
qa.a: Each twin has her own temperament: Bhavna is bold, while Alka is slower to warm up.

grounding: It shows two toddlers with different baseline reactivity and adaptability.

passage:
"Arohi, it's just the pressure cooker," Jasleen said, but Arohi was already under the table, hands over her ears.

"Too loud! Too loud!"

"Okay, okay." Jasleen crouched. "Want to come to the balcony till it's done?"

Arohi nodded and climbed into her arms.

On the balcony, Arohi's Papa called from inside, "She's so sensitive. Her cousin sleeps through fireworks."

"She's just made differently," Jasleen said. "Next time I'll take her out before the whistle."

qa.q: What sound made Arohi hide under the table?
qa.a: The pressure cooker whistle made her hide.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling under the table?
qa.a: She felt overwhelmed and frightened by the loud sound, covering her ears and saying it was too loud.

qa.q: What plan did Jasleen make, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: She decided to take Arohi outside before the whistle next time, which works with Arohi's sensitivity instead of forcing her to endure it.

qa.q: How does Arohi's Papa seem to see her reaction?
qa.a: He compares her to her cousin and seems a bit puzzled or worried that she reacts so strongly.

grounding: A home dialogue shows a toddler's strong sensitivity to noise and an adult adapting to her temperament.

passage:
Note from Vaibhav, playgroup teacher, Monday:

Suraj, two and a half, is our slow-to-warm-up friend. He stands at the door for about ten minutes each morning, watching, before he joins. At music time today he covered his ears when the drum started, but he tapped softly on the table with one finger. Scratchy labels bother him too.

What I did next: I let him watch first, gave him a small soft shaker instead of the drum, and asked his parents about his clothes.

qa.q: What did Suraj do when the drum started?
qa.a: He covered his ears but tapped softly on the table with one finger.

qa.q: What does Suraj's soft tapping suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted to join the music but felt overwhelmed by the drum's loudness, so he joined in a quieter way.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav adjust things for Suraj's temperament?
qa.a: Vaibhav let Suraj watch before joining and gave him a softer shaker, respecting his pace and sensitivity.

qa.q: How might Suraj's parents see this note?
qa.a: They may feel reassured that the teacher understands their son and is working with his needs.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a toddler's cautious, sound- and touch-sensitive temperament and how the teacher adjusted.

passage:
At the wedding in their village near Jhansi, the brass band started up, and two-year-old Divyansh clapped his hands over his ears and screamed.
His baby cousin slept straight through it on an aunt's shoulder.
Uma picked Divyansh up and carried him out behind the cowshed, where it was quieter. She hummed softly. He took his hands off his ears and leaned on her.
“You don't like loud things,” she murmured. “That's okay. We'll watch from here.”

qa.q: Where did Uma carry Divyansh?
qa.a: She carried him out behind the cowshed, where it was quieter.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel when the band started?
qa.a: He was overwhelmed and frightened by the loud noise, covering his ears and screaming.

qa.q: What did Uma do that suited Divyansh's temperament?
qa.a: She took him somewhere quieter and hummed softly instead of forcing him to stay.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's reaction differ from his cousin's, and why?
qa.a: His cousin slept through it because each child has a different sensitivity to noise.

grounding: A mother responds to her toddler's sensitivity to loud noise at a village wedding.

passage:
At the Saturday playgroup in Hanoi, Kwame ran straight to the sandpit, threw sand in the air, and laughed.
Bao, the same age, stood at the edge holding his father's leg. He watched for ten minutes. Then he touched the sand with one finger. Then he sat down, slowly.
“He takes his time,” Bao's father said to Kwame's mother.
“Kwame never does,” she laughed.
By the end, both boys were filling the same bucket.

qa.q: How long did Bao watch before touching the sand?
qa.a: He watched for ten minutes.

qa.q: How was Bao feeling at the edge of the sandpit?
qa.a: He felt cautious and a bit unsure, holding his father's leg while he watched.

qa.q: How can Bao's father support Bao's temperament?
qa.a: He can let Bao warm up at his own pace without pushing, as he did.

qa.q: How do the parents see the difference between their boys?
qa.a: They see it calmly and with humour, accepting that each boy has his own way.

grounding: Two toddlers with different temperaments approach a new sandpit in their own way.

passage:
I'm Sudha, Arnab's mashi. On the first day of Durga Puja, I watched Arnab, two, in his new silk kurta.
He pulled at the collar, scratched his neck, then threw himself on the floor and wailed.
I took the kurta off and put him in his soft cotton vest. He stopped crying almost at once and ran to see the drums.
Maybe the silk scratched. I can't say for sure. But he loves the dhak.

qa.q: What did Sudha put Arnab in instead of the kurta?
qa.a: Sudha put him in his soft cotton vest.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel in his new silk kurta?
qa.a: He seemed uncomfortable and upset, pulling at it and wailing.

qa.q: What can Arnab's family do next Puja?
qa.a: They could choose soft cotton clothes for him so he can enjoy the festival.

qa.q: What would change if Sudha had left the silk kurta on?
qa.a: Arnab might have stayed upset and itchy and missed enjoying the dhak drums.

grounding: An aunt notices a toddler's sensitivity to scratchy clothes during Durga Puja.

passage:
Two days before Holi, dhol practice started in the lane. Tarun, two, covered his ears and buried his face in Rajni's sari.
On Holi morning, Rajni kept him on the balcony. When a cousin came up with wet colour, he screamed, so Rajni put just a little dry pink gulal on his cheek. He touched it and stayed calm.
A week later, he found the small dhol in the cupboard and tapped it very softly.

qa.q: Where did Rajni keep Tarun on Holi morning?
qa.a: On the balcony.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he screamed at the wet colour?
qa.a: Tarun seemed frightened and overwhelmed by the wet, sudden touch, which was too much for him.

qa.q: Which choices by Rajni suited Tarun, and why?
qa.a: Watching from the balcony and using a little dry gulal let Tarun join the festival at a level his senses could handle.

qa.q: What would change if Tarun's cousin had kept putting wet colour on him?
qa.a: Tarun would likely become more upset and might start to dread festivals, instead of slowly getting curious about the dhol.

grounding: Over a Holi week a sound- and touch-sensitive toddler joins in on his own terms.

passage:
The first monsoon rain hit the colony. Pema, two, ran straight into the puddles by the gate, laughing and stamping.
Her neighbour Jomon, the same age, stood in the doorway and howled. His socks were wet. He tugged at them and would not move.
Jomon's father took the socks off and dried his feet. Jomon calmed, then watched Pema from the step.
"Same rain," Pema's mother said, smiling. "Two very different children."

qa.q: Where did Pema run when the rain started?
qa.a: Straight into the puddles by the gate.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he tugged at his wet socks?
qa.a: Jomon felt upset and uncomfortable; the wet socks bothered him far more than the rain bothered Pema.

qa.q: What did Jomon's father get right?
qa.a: Jomon's father dealt with the wet socks that were bothering him, instead of telling him to be like Pema.

qa.q: How does Pema's mother see the two children?
qa.a: Pema's mother sees that each child reacts in their own way to the same rain, and doesn't judge either of them.

grounding: Two toddlers show different sensory thresholds and reactions to the same monsoon rain.

passage:
"Why is Himani crying again?" asked Chachi as the wedding band started up outside.
"It's the band," said Kavitha, rocking her. "Every loud sound, she startles."
"My boys slept through all of it at this age."
"Himani doesn't. She likes quiet songs, soft light."
"She'll have to get used to it."
"Slowly, maybe." Kavitha carried Himani to the back room and hummed. Himani's fists opened.
Chachi peeped in. "Oh. She's fine now."
"She's fine here," Kavitha said softly.

qa.q: Who was rocking Himani when the band started?
qa.a: Kavitha.

qa.q: What does Himani's fists opening in the back room suggest?
qa.a: Himani is starting to feel calm and safe once the loud noise is further away.

qa.q: What could Kavitha try during the rest of the wedding?
qa.a: Kavitha could keep a quiet room ready, bring Himani out for short times, and take her back when she startles.

qa.q: Why might Chachi react differently to Himani's crying?
qa.a: Chachi's own children slept through noise, so she expects every baby to get used to it quickly.

grounding: A sensitive toddler startles at wedding noise and her mother adjusts to her needs.

Nursery note, winter festival week
Sunaina (2 years 4 months) covered her ears and hid under the table when the school band played for the winter festival. She cried until I took her outside.
Her friend Ritu danced right in front of the drums.
Sunaina is often sensitive to loud sounds and new textures. I have told her mother and suggested she bring ear muffs next time. We'll let Sunaina watch from further away.

qa.q: Where did Sunaina hide when the band played?
qa.a: Under the table.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when the band played?
qa.a: She felt frightened and overwhelmed, covering her ears and crying.

qa.q: What is the teacher planning to help Sunaina?
qa.a: Ear muffs and watching from further away, respecting her sensitivity.

qa.q: How might Ritu experience the same band?
qa.a: Ritu seems to enjoy it, dancing near the drums, showing a different temperament.

grounding: A nursery note shows a toddler's sensitivity to loud sound compared with a peer.

passage:
On a rainy spring morning in Moscow, Ivan, eighteen months, refused his new raincoat. He screamed when the plastic touched his arms.
His father Siddiq tried again. Ivan arched his back.
Siddiq stopped. He wrapped Ivan in his soft old jacket instead and held an umbrella.
Ivan quietened. He watched the rain drip off the umbrella's edge, calm now.

qa.q: What did Ivan refuse to wear?
qa.a: His new raincoat.

qa.q: How did Ivan feel when the plastic touched his arms?
qa.a: He felt upset and uncomfortable, screaming and arching his back.

qa.q: What did Siddiq do that suited Ivan's temperament?
qa.a: He stopped forcing the raincoat and used the soft jacket and umbrella instead.

qa.q: How might Siddiq feel after Ivan quietens?
qa.a: Siddiq probably feels relieved and learns what textures bother Ivan.

grounding: Shows a toddler's sensory sensitivity to a new texture and a caregiver adapting.

passage:
I'm Ojas, the uncle next door, and I was at the birthday party on Sunday. When the first balloon popped, little Jagdish, two, clapped both hands over his ears and buried his face in his mother's neck. His cousin Tara, the same age, ran toward the noise shouting "More!"
Jagdish stayed on his mother's lap for most of the party. Later, in the quiet bedroom, he stacked blocks for a long time and smiled at me.
I don't know exactly what he felt. They're just made differently, I think.

qa.q: What did Tara shout when the balloon popped?
qa.a: She ran toward the noise shouting "More!"

qa.q: What might Jagdish have been feeling when he covered his ears?
qa.a: He was probably startled and overwhelmed by the loud popping, and he sought comfort from his mother.

qa.q: How could Jagdish's family help him at noisy events?
qa.a: They could let him arrive early, keep a quiet room nearby for breaks, and let him join at his own pace instead of pushing him into the noise.

qa.q: How does Ojas see the difference between the two cousins?
qa.a: Ojas sees that the two children react very differently to the same noise and thinks they are simply made differently, without judging either one.

grounding: Shows a toddler's sensitive temperament to loud sounds, contrasted with a cousin who enjoys noise.
